text:
Predicates:
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
Schedule(x) ::: x schedules a meeting with their customers.
Appears(x) ::: x appears in the company today.
HasLunchInCompany(x) ::: x has lunch in the company.
HasLunchAtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
WorksRemotely(x) ::: x is working remotely from home.
InOtherCountry(x) ::: x is in another country.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
Premises:
∀x (Employee(x) ∧ Schedule(x) → Appears(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will appear in the company today.
∀x (HasLunchInCompany(x) → Schedule(x)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (Employee(x) → HasLunchInCompany(x) ⊕ HasLunchAtHome(x)) ::: Employees will either have lunch in the company or have lunch at home.
∀x (HasLunchAtHome(x) → WorksRemotely(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, then he/she is working remotely from home.
∀x (InOtherCountry(x) → WorksRemotely(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
∀x (Manager(x) → ¬WorksRemotely(x)) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
(Manager(james) ∧ Appears(james)) ⊕ ¬(Manager(james) ∨ Appears(james)) ::: James is either a manager and appears in the company today or neither a manager nor appears in the company today.
Conclusion:
HasLunchInCompany(james) ::: James has lunch in the company.
